solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Binding refusal time after time in Lear, perhaps

indicators.note: 'in' puts the refusal and the two times inside the king, as a passenger sits in a car

parts.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's tragic king; 'perhaps' marks him as one example

indicators.note: 'after' sets one time behind the other, so the Ts stand side by side

explanation.surface: An actor playing Lear keeps saying no, over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time after time' sounds like 'repeatedly' but is simply two Ts in a row; 'perhaps' warns that Lear stands for any king.
explanation.definitionFit: Tying knots in rope or string is a way of fastening, so the binding here is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Girl recruiting soldiers for unarmed combat

explanation.surface: A young woman signs up troops to learn fighting without weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recruiting' fits the army surface so well that it hides its job of putting one thing inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese martial art uses hands and feet only, which is what 'unarmed' describes.

clue.text: Boundless woodland hosting private revels

indicators.note: a word without its bounds has lost its edges, the first and last letters
a host has guests inside, so the trimmed wood holds the private

parts.note: fOREST without its first and last letters
a GI is an American private soldier

explanation.surface: Wild parties are held deep in an endless forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like part of the definition, private revels, but it is an American soldier and belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Revels are riotous merrymaking, and orgies are the wildest kind of it, so the definition is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Banker on board named in official document

indicators.note: a passenger on board a ship is inside it, so the river goes inside

parts.note: a banker is something with banks, a river: the Dee

explanation.surface: A banker who sits on a company board is listed in an official paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' is the crossword river, something that has banks; the surface wants a financier sitting on a board of directors.
explanation.definitionFit: The paper proving who owns a property is a legal record, an official document by any measure.

clue.text: Handles aren't designed for old people

indicators.note: something designed has been made into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that door handles are not made for elderly hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about the elderly; the 'old people' are old in the prehistoric sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct humans lived tens of thousands of years ago, so they are old people in the long sense rather than elderly.

clue.text: Breathing apparatus that is help to anglers

parts.note: a fish breathes through its gills

explanation.surface: Some breathing kit is the thing to help people fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: A gillie is the Scottish attendant who guides anglers and deer stalkers; the fish's gill makes a neat link with the anglers.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Help' is used as a noun for a helper, and the Scottish attendant on fishing trips is exactly that.

clue.text: Best clue last of all

parts.note: a clue is an idea, as in 'I haven't a clue'

indicators.note: 'last of' a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: The finest crossword clue is the one saved till the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last of all' reads as 'finally'; it is the letter that ends 'all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perfect for the purpose is the best possible, a plain adjective synonym.

clue.text: Part played by staff official staying in touch

parts.note: an actor's part is his lines

explanation.surface: An official plays a role while keeping in contact with colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In touch' means beside the touchline, where the linesman runs, not keeping contact.
explanation.definitionFit: The assistant referee runs along the touchline, the edge of the pitch, so he stays in touch literally.

clue.text: English graduate put off motherhood for ages

indicators.note: a passenger put off a bus is removed, so the graduate leaves the word

parts.note: motherhood = maternity, which loses MA to leave TERNITY

explanation.surface: An English graduate delays starting a family for years.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a woman postponing having children; 'put off' really means removal.
explanation.definitionFit: 'For ages' and 'for an eternity' both mean for a very long time, an everyday exaggeration.

clue.text: Sporting greats at sporting events

indicators.note: sporting can mean frolicking, and letters at play jump about into a new order

explanation.surface: Sports legends turn up at competitions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' appears twice, once as the anagram signal and once in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Boat races held as a series make a day of rowing or sailing competition, an example of sporting events.

clue.text: Late attendees here may be expected to knock

definitions.text: Late attendees here may be expected to knock

parts.note: the surface reading is people arriving after the start; the setter means the dead, the late

parts.words: here may be expected to knock
parts.note: a latecomer knocks at the door; a spirit raps on the table to show it has come

explanation.surface: Latecomers somewhere are expected to knock before entering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means dead, not tardy: spirits called up at a seance are said to knock to show they are there.
explanation.definitionFit: At a sitting to contact the dead, the spirits traditionally announce themselves by rapping.

clue.text: US city Xmas visitor eating a couple of cakes

indicators.note: what you eat goes inside you, so Santa takes the rest in

parts.note: a cake of soap is a bar, so two cakes make BAR BAR

explanation.surface: Father Christmas stops off in an American city and has some cake.
explanation.walkthrough: The cakes are not food but cakes of soap, which are bars; the surface makes Santa hungry to hide that.
explanation.definitionFit: The Californian coastal city is named after a saint, and 'US city' is a plain definition by category.

clue.text: Subject of article by yours truly

explanation.surface: A writer asks what her own article is about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a piece of journalism; it is the grammar word.
explanation.definitionFit: The topic running through an essay or talk is its subject, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Pride, say, is Lady Enid's failing

indicators.note: letters that are failing break down, and fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A titled lady's weakness is her vanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failing' is a noun in the surface, Lady Enid's flaw; in the wordplay it is a verb breaking her letters up.
explanation.definitionFit: Pride heads the traditional list of seven sins, so 'Pride, say' is a definition by example.

clue.text: Candid judge to put in the painting

indicators.note: 'to put in the' tells you to insert 'to' into 'the'

parts.note: as written, which takes TO after its T

explanation.surface: A frank critic is asked to judge a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The little words 'to' and 'the' look like grammar glue, but both are letters used as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A talk between two people that is open and honest is candid, so the phrase works as an adjective here.

clue.text: Cellular structure that's bony treated with chemo

indicators.note: something treated has been processed and changed, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A medical note about bone tissue receiving chemotherapy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cellular' pulls toward biology and cancer; the cells are the wax hexagons of a beehive.
explanation.definitionFit: Bees build rows of six-sided wax cells, so the thing is literally a structure of cells.

clue.text: Trumpet, for one, in shortened grip

indicators.note: 'in' places the one inside the grip
a word shortened has lost its tail, its final letter

parts.note: a clamp grips; shortened to CLAM

explanation.surface: A trumpet is an example of something held in a short grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For one' looks like 'for example' after Trumpet, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To trumpet news is to announce it loudly, and the verb here is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Satisfied rebel after heartless monarch died

indicators.note: a heartless word has lost its heart, the middle letter
'after' puts the rebel behind the monarch

parts.note: d = died, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A rebel is content once a cruel king has died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' reads as cruel but empties the monarch of her middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A thirst that is quenched has been satisfied, so the past participle matches the adjective.

clue.text: Crazy pin position on a dogleg hole

definitions.text: pin position on a dogleg hole
definitions.meaning: a dogleg is a golf hole that turns partway, so the flag is out of sight past the corner

explanation.surface: A golfer complains about a mad flag placement.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf the pin is the flagstick, and a dogleg is a hole that bends left or right.
explanation.definitionFit: Round the bend is British slang for mad, and on a dogleg the flag sits literally round the bend.

clue.text: Block hosting jazz regularly and a market

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the block holds the rest
at regular intervals, so every other letter

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of jAzZ

explanation.surface: An apartment block puts on jazz nights and a street market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' is a verb, to bar, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: An eastern market street full of stalls, and by extension any sale of goods, so a plain synonym.

clue.text: Key to a vacant penthouse getaway

parts.note: the Esc key on a keyboard

indicators.note: a vacant flat is emptied, so only the outer letters stay

explanation.surface: A key to an empty top-floor flat offers a way out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' pulls toward a door key; it is the computer key.
explanation.definitionFit: A getaway is a flight from danger or the law, which is exactly what this word means.

clue.text: Agreement, mostly about beer, covering make-up

indicators.note: most of a word, but not all, so its last letter is dropped
'about' means around, so the shortened word wraps round the beer

parts.note: CONCERT (agreement, as in 'acting in concert') without its last letter

explanation.surface: A deal about beer also covers cosmetics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering' looks like a container signal but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cosmetic is dabbed on to hide spots and dark circles, so it is make-up that covers.

clue.text: Large birds caught in nets

indicators.note: the birds have caught the next letter and hold it inside

parts.note: a = in, as in 'twice a day' or 'abed'

explanation.surface: Big birds are trapped in netting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nets' looks like the trap; it is the verb, to make money. 'In' giving A is rare: the old prefix of abed and asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To net a sum is to take it home as profit, so the verb is a plain synonym.

clue.text: A poet still nursing a son

indicators.note: a nurse holds a baby in her arms, so the word holds the A

explanation.surface: A poet still cradles his infant son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' pulls toward 'motionless'; it is the adverb meaning 'even now'.
explanation.definitionFit: W. B. Yeats, the Irish Nobel laureate, is a definition by example of a poet.

clue.text: Keep a present for daughter to open

indicators.note: the daughter stands at the opening of 'here', its front

parts.note: present = here, as in a register

explanation.surface: A gift for a daughter to unwrap is something to keep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' is the gift in the surface but the word meaning 'in attendance' in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The fit comes through 'keep to': to keep to a rule is to stick with it, the same sense as the answer.

clue.text: Prospect of a country containing gold

indicators.note: the country contains the gold, holding it inside

explanation.surface: A nation's prospects depend on its gold reserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prospect' suggests future chances and gold-prospecting; here it is a view.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospect in its older sense is a wide view over the landscape, a sweeping vista.

clue.text: Simple ways back from defeat

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Humble routes back after a loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' suggests a reversal but only takes the end letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain, unpretentious lodgings or means are both simple and humble, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Drunken mob jeer a carnival

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of line, so the letters lose their order

explanation.surface: A drunk crowd heckles a street parade.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole scene is a rowdy carnival, so the definition hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A big noisy celebration or gathering, such as a Scout rally, is a carnival in the loose sense.
